sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Individual consumers will adopt a consumer-facing deposit return system if it offers a convenient, digital refund mechanism and a clear path to return containers, because convenience and digital payout reduce the effort and friction of the return process. Who benefits: Households that need to return beverage containers and receive immediate digital refunds.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers currently face the hassle of visiting a physical return point or redemption center. A digital app that allows returns and refunds online removes this friction, making recycling more convenient and attractive.. How value is captured: TOMRA can capture value by selling the app as a subscription or one-time purchase, earning recurring revenue from refunds and potentially charging for premium features like loyalty points or bundled recycling services.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay for a digital refund service.; The digital platform can be integrated with existing deposit return infrastructure without major hardware changes.; Regulatory requirements allow digital payout of refunds.. Predictions: In a test market, households using the digital app will return containers at a higher rate than those using only physical return points.; Willingness to pay for the digital service will be above a threshold of €5 per return, based on survey data.; Adoption will be higher in regions with strong deposit return participation (e.g., New South Wales, Ireland)..

T2: Individual consumers will adopt a consumer-facing deposit return system if it offers a reward mechanism (e.g., loyalty points, discounts) tied to returned containers, because the tangible incentive motivates repeat behavior and increases the perceived value of recycling. Who benefits: Households that return containers for rewards, not just for the deposit refund.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers are motivated by immediate benefits rather than abstract environmental goals. A reward system creates a personal incentive to recycle, making the act of returning containers feel rewarding rather than mandatory.. How value is captured: TOMRA can capture value by partnering with retailers to offer reward points or discounts, and by selling a subscription-based loyalty platform that earns revenue from reward redemptions.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to trade a small refund for a reward.; The reward mechanism can be integrated into the existing deposit return infrastructure without major changes.; Retailers will partner to promote the reward program.. Predictions: In a test market, households receiving rewards will return containers at a higher rate than those receiving only a refund.; Willingness to pay for the reward program will be above a threshold of 5% of the refund amount, based on survey data.; Adoption will be higher in regions with strong deposit return participation where consumers already shop frequently at return points..

Test "Digital vs Reward Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey experiment with two arms: Arm A receives a digital refund mechanism (app-based) and Arm B receives a reward mechanism (loyalty points/discounts). Participants are recruited from households in regions with strong deposit return participation (e.g., New South Wales, Ireland). Each arm presents a scenario where participants must return beverage containers and choose the return method.. Sample: 500 households (250 per arm) recruited via an online panel, balanced across the two regions.. Measure: Primary measure: proportion of participants choosing the digital refund mechanism (Arm A) versus the reward mechanism (Arm B). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) for the digital refund service (WTP per return).. Predictions: T1: Arm A will have a higher proportion of participants choosing the digital refund mechanism than Arm B, and WTP for the digital service will be above €5 per return.; T2: Arm B will have a higher proportion of participants choosing the reward mechanism than Arm A, and WTP for the reward program will be above 5% of the refund amount.. Decision rule: If the observed proportion of participants choosing the digital refund mechanism in Arm A is at least 15 percentage points higher than in Arm B, conclude T1 is supported. If the observed proportion of participants choosing the reward mechanism in Arm B is at least 15 percentage points higher than in Arm A, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 15 percentage points, both theories remain plausible and further testing is needed.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that offers a digital refund mechanism, leveraging TOMRA’s existing app and digital payout capabilities. This aligns with evidence of consumer convenience and digital refund adoption, while addressing the lack of reward mechanism support. Conduct a small-scale pilot to validate willingness to pay and return rates before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated result (SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE) does not address digital refund mechanisms or reward mechanisms, so it does not affect T1. New claim: Individual consumers will adopt a consumer-facing deposit return system if it offers a convenient, digital refund mechanism and a clear path to return containers, because convenience and digital payout reduce the effort and friction of the return process.. Evidence: SYN-TOMRA-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that offers a digital refund mechanism, leveraging TOMRA’s existing app and digital payout capabilities. This aligns with evidence of consumer convenience and digital refund adoption, while addressing the lack of reward mechanism support. Conduct a small-scale pilot to validate willingness to pay and return rates before scaling. Target customer: Households that need to return beverage containers and receive immediate digital refunds, particularly in regions with strong deposit return participation (e.g., New South Wales, Ireland).. Value proposition: A digital app that allows returns and refunds online, reducing friction and offering immediate digital payout of refunds, making recycling more convenient and attractive to individual consumers.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Digital vs Reward Test (500 households, 6 weeks, €8,000) to measure return method choice and willingness to pay for the digital refund service. Use the 15‑percentage‑point difference rule to decide whether to proceed with a. Uncertainty: The evidence does not show whether consumers would be motivated by rewards or whether they would pay for a reward mechanism. The pilot will address this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the pilot shows the reward mechanism (Arm B) achieving a 15‑percentage‑point higher choice rate than the digital refund mechanism (Arm A), we would shift focus to reward mechanisms and consider a reward‑based proposition.; If the pilot shows no significant difference in choice rates between the digital refund and reward mechanisms, we would remain committed to the digital refund mechanism and not pursue reward mechanisms.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Simplified vs Modular CNC" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase intent. Participants view two product concepts: (1) Simplified CNC router marketed as easy-to-use for home projects (2) Modular CNC router marketed as adaptable for multiple materials. Participants indicate willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent on a 7-point scale. The test also collects demographic data (age, occupation, DIY experience).. Sample: 200 participants: 100 self-identified DIY woodworkers (recruited via woodworking forums and social media) and 100 small-batch manufacturers/hobbyists (recruited via makerspace networks and industry forums). Randomly assigned to view either the simplified or modular concept first.. Measure: Average WTP (EUR) and purchase intent score (1‑7) for each concept.. Predictions: T1: DIY woodworkers will show higher WTP and purchase intent for the simplified concept (WTP ≥ €1,200 and intent ≥ 5/7) compared to the modular concept.; T2: Small-batch manufacturers/hobbyists will show higher WTP and purchase intent for the modular concept (WTP ≥ €1,500 and intent ≥ 5/7) compared to the simplified concept.. Decision rule: If simplified WTP ≥ €1,200 and intent ≥ 5/7 among DIY woodworkers, proceed with a consumer-friendly proposition (supports T1). If modular WTP ≥ €1,500 and intent ≥ 5/7 among small-batch manufacturers/hobbyists, proceed with a modular proposition (supports T2). If neither meets thresholds, recommend no expansion. If both meet thresholds, prioritize the segment with the highest. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for simplified vs modular concepts before committing resources. If the test meets the defined thresholds, proceed with a consumer-friendly proposition; otherwise, maintain the current B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Who benefits: Hobbyists and small workshops that need precise, repeatable results for home projects.. Why behaviour changes: They are willing to pay a premium for machines that meet professional standards, even if the price is higher than generic hobbyist tools.. How value is captured: Biesse can capture value by selling premium-priced machines and offering advanced features, service contracts, and training to justify the higher cost.. Why behaviour changes: They are willing to pay a premium for machines that use energy-efficient components, recycled materials, and offer carbon-neutral production, reflecting their values.. How value is captured: Biesse can capture value by positioning its machines as sustainable, offering eco-certifications, and potentially charging a premium for green branding, while also meeting regulatory requirements.. Assumptions: Eco-conscious consumers are a growing segment in the hobbyist market.; Sustainability is a meaningful purchase driver for hobbyists.; Biesse can differentiate through eco-friendly features without compromising performance.. Predictions: Eco-conscious hobbyists will show higher purchase intent or actual purchases of Biesse machines compared to non-eco-friendly alternatives.; Surveyed hobbyists will rank sustainability higher than price or performance.; Sales of eco-focused Biesse models will increase in regions with strong environmental awareness..

Sample: 300 respondents: 150 self-identified hobbyists and small workshop owners (recruited via DIY forums and social media).. Predictions: T1: Hobbyists will show higher WTP for the premium professional-grade machine compared to the eco-friendly machine.; T2: Hobbyists will show higher WTP for the eco-friendly machine compared to the premium professional-grade machine.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the premium professional-grade machine exceeds the average WTP for the eco-friendly machine by at least 10 percentage points, conclude T1 is supported. If the average WTP for the eco-friendly machine exceeds the premium professional-grade machine by at least 10 percentage points, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is within 10 percentage points, the test is inconclusive and further market research is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Test "Hobbyist Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a sample of 300 hobbyists (recruited via metalworking forums and social media). Participants view two product concepts for a CNC mill: (A) Functional-focused, emphasizing reliability, affordability, and space efficiency; (B) Lifestyle-focused, emphasizing status, craftsmanship, and community recognition. They are asked to choose which concept they would buy and to rate their willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale. They also. Sample: 300 hobbyists (150 per condition) recruited via metalworking forums and social media, balanced for age, gender, and experience level.. Measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants choosing Concept A versus Concept B. Secondary outcomes: average WTP for each concept, and self-reported importance of functional vs. status attributes.. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of participants will choose Concept A (functional) and average WTP for Concept A will be at least €1,500 higher than for Concept B.; T2: At least 60% of participants will choose Concept B (lifestyle) and average WTP for Concept B will be at least €1,500 higher than for Concept A.. Decision rule: If the observed choice proportion for Concept A exceeds 55% and the WTP difference between concepts is at least €1,500, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting functional need. If Concept B exceeds 55% and the WTP difference is at least €1,500, . Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Hobbyist Preference Test (X1) to empirically compare functional vs. lifestyle positioning. If the test shows a ≥55% choice for the functional concept and a WTP difference of ≥€1,500, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists' functional needs. If not, maintain the current B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer vs Small Business Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a consumer-focused vacuum sealer description emphasizing professional-grade sous vide sealing and bulk food processing. Group B sees a small business-focused vacuum sealer description emphasizing labor cost savings, faster packaging, and improved product freshness. Both groups see a neutral product description as a control. Participants are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 300 participants: 150 home cooks/culinary enthusiasts and 150 small businesses/direct sellers, recruited via online panels to ensure diversity in demographics and purchase intent.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum willingness to pay (EUR) for each group.. Predictions: T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Group B.; T2: Group B will have higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than Group A.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), we conclude T1 is supported. If Group B’s score is at least 1.5 points higher and the difference is statistically significant, we conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference is statistically significant, we conclude neither theory is supported and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine for residential deposit return if they perceive a convenient, immediate digital refund and a clear map to collection points, because they value the ease of refunding containers without retailer involvement. Who benefits: Individual consumers receiving digital refunds quickly and easily.. Why behaviour changes: The removal of retailer obligations in some jurisdictions (e.g., New South Wales DRS) creates a demand for consumer‑friendly refund mechanisms; consumers are accustomed to app‑based digital payouts and will switch if they see the same. How value is captured: TOMRA captures value by charging consumers a small fee for each container deposited and by selling data on recycling volume to municipalities or manufacturers.. Assumptions: Consumers trust that digital refunds will be honored.; There is sufficient consumer awareness and access to the app in target markets.; Competition from other refund mechanisms (e.g., cash redemption) is limited.. Predictions: A test group offered the app will show a higher proportion of containers deposited compared to a control group without the app.; Surveyed consumers will rate the app’s ease of refund as “very easy” or “easily possible” at a rate above 60%..

T2: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine for residential deposit return if they receive a tangible reward (e.g., points, discounts, or loyalty credits) that can be redeemed for goods or services, because they value the additional incentive beyond the refund. Who benefits: Individual consumers receiving a tangible reward.. Why behaviour changes: Tangible rewards create a direct financial benefit that motivates consumers to actively return containers, especially when combined with convenience (e.g., app‑based deposit tracking).. How value is captured: TOMRA captures value by partnering with retailers or service providers to offer rewards, and by selling aggregated recycling data to manufacturers or municipalities.. Assumptions: Consumers trust that rewards will be honored and are aware of redemption options.; Retailers or service providers are willing to partner to offer rewards.; Competition from cash redemption or other refund mechanisms is not sufficient to offset the reward incentive.. Predictions: A test group offered a reward system will show a higher proportion of containers deposited compared to a control group without rewards.; Surveyed consumers will rate the reward system as “very attractive” or “easily attractive” at a rate above 55%..

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Direct‑to‑Consumer Offering vs Subscription Model" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view a product description of a compact automated storage unit (specifications, benefits, price). They are then presented with two purchase options: (A) Direct‑purchase at full price (EUR 1,500), (B) Subscription‑based offering with monthly fee (EUR 50) and installation/maintenance included. They choose which option they would select and provide a brief explanation. The test is run with 200 participants (100 per arm) over 12 weeks.. Sample: 200 homeowners and small‑business owners recruited via online panels, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Purchase intent (percentage selecting option A or B) and primary reason cited for choice (e.g., "direct purchase cheaper," "subscription reduces upfront cost").. Predictions: T1: Direct‑purchase intent ≥ 40% and subscription intent ≤ 30% (favors T1).; T2: Subscription intent ≥ 40% and direct purchase intent ≤ 30% (favors T2).. Decision rule: If direct‑purchase intent ≥ 40% and subscription intent ≤ 30%, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home storage (supports T1). If subscription intent ≥ 40% and direct purchase intent ≤ 30%, develop a subscription‑based service (supports T2). If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to validate demand and willingness to pay for a direct‑purchase model before committing resources. If the test shows direct‑purchase intent ≥ 40% and subscription intent ≤ 30%, proceed with a home‑storage offering; otherwise, maintain current B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Nabtesco Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing precision reduction gears, automatic doors, transport equipment and welfare components sold to manufacturers, building owners and transport operators? sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Biesse S.p.A. investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.; Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable path to capture value from individual consumers.; Any recommendation must consider Biesse’s existing B2B customer base and current product portfolio.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting individual hobbyists, DIY enthusiasts, or small workshops for a specific use case (e.g., home furniture making, small woodwork).; 2) Expand the existing B2B product line into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑friendly features to existing machines).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B market and existing product portfolio.; 4) Target a new consumer segment with a different value proposition (e.g., eco‑friendly, smart manufacturing, or subscription services) while retaining the core B2B business..

T1: Individual hobbyists and small workshops purchase CNC machines for creative projects, so a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home furniture making, small woodwork) would generate demand. Who benefits: Hobbyists and small workshops gain affordable access to professional-grade CNC tools for custom projects.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently lack affordable entry into CNC machining, so a consumer-friendly proposition that simplifies operation and targeting specific projects would increase adoption.. How value is captured: Biesse would sell differentiated consumer models at premium prices, capturing margin on a niche segment while maintaining its B2B core.. Assumptions: Hobbyists and small workshops are a large enough segment to justify development costs.; A differentiated use case proposition (e.g., simplified interface, modular tooling) can be engineered without major redesign.; Consumers are willing to pay for perceived professional quality in a compact form.. Predictions: In a pilot offering a simplified desktop CNC for hobbyists, at least 10% of surveyed participants would express intent to purchase within 6 months.; Sales conversion rate would exceed 5% of surveyed interest, indicating meaningful demand..

T2: Individual buyers purchase CNC machines to reduce labor costs and improve efficiency in small-scale production, so a consumer proposition focused on cost savings and simplified operation would drive demand. Who benefits: Small workshops and individual producers gain lower labor costs and faster production cycles.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently outsource CNC work or use manual methods, so a proposition that lowers operational costs and simplifies setup would make the machine attractive.. How value is captured: Biesse would sell consumer models at lower margins but higher volume, leveraging its existing B2B distribution to reach individual buyers.. Assumptions: Small-scale producers have budget constraints that make a consumer-grade CNC affordable.; Simplified operation (e.g., plug-and-play, lower setup time) can be achieved without major redesign.; Labor cost savings are a primary purchase driver for this segment.. Predictions: In a pilot offering a simplified desktop CNC priced at a consumer-friendly rate, at least 15% of surveyed participants would indicate intent to purchase within 6 months.; Sales conversion rate would exceed 8% of surveyed interest, indicating meaningful demand..

T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition for home storage primarily if the solution is marketed as a premium, integrated smart system that solves a specific pain point (e.g., space optimization or inventory management) and is delivered through a dedicated consumer brand and direct-to-consumer channels. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking efficient storage solutions and Kardex through premium pricing and brand equity in a new consumer segment.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers increasingly seek integrated smart home solutions that automate and optimize daily tasks; a differentiated proposition that addresses a clear consumer need and is positioned as a premium, easy-to-use product will attract those who. How value is captured: Kardex captures value through higher margins from direct-to-consumer sales, subscription services for software/data, and optional add‑ons, leveraging existing manufacturing capabilities to produce a consumer‑specific product.. Assumptions: There is sufficient consumer awareness and willingness to pay for automated home storage solutions.; Kardex can adapt its existing manufacturing and service infrastructure to serve the consumer market.; Distribution partners will be willing to take on a consumer brand and dedicated sales channels.. Predictions: A consumer proposition marketed as a premium smart storage system will achieve at least 10% higher willingness-to-pay than comparable non-smart storage products.; Purchase intent will be higher among households with a higher proportion of tech‑savvy occupants (e.g., millennials) or those seeking space optimization.; Repeat purchase rate for subscription services (e.g., data management or software updates) will be at least 30% within 12 months of initial purchase..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition for home storage primarily if the solution is bundled with a leading consumer brand (e.g., IKEA, Amazon) that already owns a consumer-facing ecosystem, leveraging existing consumer distribution and marketing channels to lower entry barriers. Who benefits: Kardex through access to established consumer markets and brand trust, and the consumer brand through a new, low-cost entry into automated storage.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers already shop at these brands and trust their product quality; bundling a storage solution with a familiar brand reduces perceived risk and simplifies purchase decisions, especially for. How value is captured: Kardex captures value through volume sales at lower margins but higher unit volume, and through optional add-ons or service contracts; the consumer brand captures value through new product category and potential cross-selling.. Assumptions: The consumer brand is willing to partner with Kardex to co-brand a storage solution.; Kardex can meet the brand’s quality and design standards for a consumer product.; Consumers will purchase the bundled product at a price point that covers Kardex’s cost and generates a modest margin for the brand.. Predictions: A bundled consumer proposition will achieve at least 20% higher purchase intent than a standalone Kardex product offered through the same channel.; The bundled product will be purchased by at least 15% of households that have previously purchased products from the partnering brand.; Repeat purchase rate for add-ons or service contracts will be at least 25% within 12 months of initial purchase..

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Test "Consumer vs Small Business Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a consumer-focused message emphasizing food freshness and waste reduction; Group B sees a small‑business‑focused message emphasizing cost savings and freshness improvement. Both groups are asked about willingness to pay (WTP) and intent to purchase.. Sample: 300 participants: 150 home cooks/culinary enthusiasts and 150 small businesses/direct sellers, recruited via online panels.. Measure: Willingness to pay (WTP) in euros and purchase intent (binary: "Would buy").. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher WTP and purchase intent than Group B.; T2: Group B will show higher WTP and purchase intent than Group A.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for Group A is at least 30% higher than Group B and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), conclude T1 is supported. If Group B's WTP is at least 30% higher and the difference is statistically significant, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the threshold, neither theory is supported.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer vacuum sealer positioned around food freshness and waste reduction, targeting serious home cooks and culinary enthusiasts. Use the existing dealer network and online channels to reach individual buyers. Conduct a small-scale messaging test (e.g., Group A vs. Group B) to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent before full-scale launch. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for a Consumer-Grade Biesse CNC Router" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are recruited from a panel of DIY woodworkers (defined as those who have built or modified wood projects in the past 12 months) and homeowners (defined as those who have undertaken home improvement projects requiring precision cutting). Each participant is shown a product description of a consumer-grade Biesse CNC router with specifications matching a desktop model (e.g., 12"x24" work. Sample: 200 participants: 100 DIY woodworkers and 100 homeowners. Recruitment via a panel provider to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros, measured as the maximum price participants would pay for the router. Secondary measures: purchase intent (binary) and perceived importance of precision and professional-grade features.. Predictions: T1: DIY woodworkers will report a WTP at least 1.5x the price of comparable consumer CNC routers (e.g., €2,500 vs €1,600).; T2: Homeowners will report a WTP at least 1.5x the price of comparable consumer CNC routers (e.g., €2,500 vs €1,600).. Decision rule: If the average WTP for DIY woodworkers exceeds €2,000 and the average WTP for homeowners exceeds €2,000, both theories are considered supported. If only one group exceeds €2,000, the theory for that group is supported, and the other is rejected. If neither group exceeds €2,000, both theories are rejected.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Conduct the proposed consumer willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether DIY woodworkers are willing to pay a premium for a consumer-grade Biesse CNC router. The survey will provide real demand evidence and help decide whether to invest in a differentiated consumer proposition or pursue other options. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Conduct the proposed consumer willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether DIY woodworkers are willing to pay a premium for a consumer-grade Biesse CNC router. Target customer: DIY woodworkers who have built or modified wood projects in the past 12 months and are willing to purchase directly from Biesse.. Value proposition: A consumer-grade Biesse CNC router that delivers professional-grade precision and digital control, sold directly to DIY woodworkers at a premium price, capturing margin on hardware and software while offering accessories and service. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 10‑week, €15,000 willingness‑to‑pay survey with 200 participants (100 DIY woodworkers, 100 homeowners). Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on DIY woodworker demand and willingness to pay a premium for a consumer‑grade router. The survey will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the survey shows average willingness‑to‑pay below €2,000 for DIY woodworkers, T1 would be rejected and the recommendation would shift to other expansion options or no expansion.; If the survey shows average willingness‑to‑pay above €2,000 for homeowners, T2 would be supported and the recommendation would shift to targeting homeowners instead of DIY woodworkers.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 32 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Biesse Hobbyist Machines" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a controlled choice experiment. Participants are recruited from a panel of individual woodworkers and hobbyists. Each participant views a product description of a Biesse desktop CNC machine and is presented with two price points: a premium price (e.g., €3,000) and a standard hobbyist price (e.g., €1,500). They are asked to indicate whether they would purchase the machine at each price point and to state their primary reason for choosing the machine.. Sample: Proposed sample: 200 participants (100 per price point) from a panel of individual woodworkers and hobbyists in the United States and Europe. Recruitment via online panels and social media groups.. Measure: Primary outcome: percentage of participants who indicate they would purchase the machine at the premium price. Secondary outcomes: proportion of participants who choose the premium price over the standard price, and self-reported primary purchase reason (precision/quality vs. community).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of participants will choose the premium price, and the premium price will be selected by a majority of respondents.; T2: At least 30% of participants will choose the premium price, but the premium price will be selected by fewer respondents than the standard price, and community reasons will be cited by a majority of premium-price buyers.. Decision rule: If the premium-price choice rate is at least 30% across both price points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the premium-price choice rate is below 30% or the standard-price choice rate is significantly higher, consider no expansion or a different value proposition. If the premium-price choice rate is between 20% and 30%, conduct a follow-up survey to validate the premium-price preference before committing to a full consumer launch.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.

Favours T1: Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (X1) to test whether individual woodworkers and hobbyists are willing to pay a premium price for Biesse machines. If the premium-price choice rate is at least 30%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists and small workshops. If the rate is below 30%, consider no expansion or a different value proposition before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (X1) to test whether individual woodworkers and hobbyists are willing to pay a premium price for Biesse machines. If the premium-price choice rate is at least 30%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists and small workshops. If the rate is below 30%, consider no expansion or a different value proposition before committing resources. Target customer: Individual woodworkers and hobbyists who value precision, quality, and professional-grade performance, and are willing to invest in machines that meet industrial standards.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions Biesse machines as premium, high-performance tools for hobbyists and small workshops, leveraging the company's reputation for quality and precision to justify premium pricing.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the willingness-to-pay survey (X1) with a sample of 200 participants, analyze results, and decide on a go/no-go basis for a consumer proposition.. Uncertainty: The size of the hobbyist market, willingness to pay a premium price, and the competitive landscape for consumer-grade CNC machines are uncertain. The survey results will be the primary source of evidence.. Would change if: If the premium-price choice rate is below 30% or the standard-price choice rate is significantly higher, indicating limited demand for a premium proposition.; If new evidence shows strong consumer demand for community and collaboration features, which would shift the value proposition toward a community-driven model.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

If the difference is less than 5 points and the sustainability scenario does not significantly outperform, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Generic Drill Bits" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 200 hobbyists and small workshop owners recruited via metalworking forums and social media, balanced across Germany and the US.. Measure: 1) Choice: which drill bit they would purchase (Gühring premium or generic alternative). 2) WTP: maximum price they would pay for the chosen brand. 3) Quality ranking (1‑10) for each brand.. Predictions: T1: At least 40% of respondents will choose Gühring premium and indicate intent to purchase, with a WTP premium of at least 20% over generic.; T2: At least 40% will choose Gühring premium and indicate intent to purchase, with a WTP premium of at least 15% over generic, achieved via existing B2B channels.. Decision rule: If the observed choice rate for Gühring premium ≥ 40% and the average WTP premium ≥ 20% (or 15% via B2B channel), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists. If either condition fails, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Lapp Home Automation" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners in Germany who own electric vehicles and have home charging installations. They are randomly assigned to one of two scenarios: (A) a premium, integrated Lapp-branded home‑automation charging kit (e.g., a cable and connector set marketed as a single, co‑branded product) priced at €250; (B) a generic Lapp cable and connector set (same technical specifications) priced at €150. Both scenarios include a brief product description emphasizing Lapp’s. Sample: 200 participants (100 per scenario) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and EV ownership status.. Measure: Primary outcome: willingness to pay (WTP) difference between the premium integrated kit and the generic kit (WTP premium). Secondary outcomes: purchase intent (binary) and perceived reliability (1‑10 scale).. Predictions: T1: WTP premium ≥ €100 (i.e., participants value the integrated premium kit at least €100 more than the generic kit).; T2: WTP premium ≤ €50 (i.e., participants do not value the integrated premium kit more than the generic kit).. Decision rule: If WTP premium ≥ €100, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium, integrated home‑automation charging. If WTP premium ≤ €50, maintain the current B2B focus. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

case.question: Should Sika AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing construction chemicals, sealants and adhesives for contractors, distributors and industrial manufacturers? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Efficiency vs Brand Prestige" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a machine marketed as efficient (e.g., "produces 30% more yarn per day"), while Group B sees a machine marketed as premium and artisan‑grade (e.g., "hand‑made design, professional‑grade quality"). Both groups view product details, price, and financing options. After viewing, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested).. Sample: 300 participants: 150 per group, recruited via a panel to match hobbyist demographics (age 25‑55, spinning experience 1‑55 years).. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑55) for each group.. Predictions: T1: Group A will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group B (difference ≥ 1.5 points).; T2: Group B will have a higher average purchase intent score than Group A (difference ≥ 1.5 points).. Decision rule: If Group A’s average score is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B’s, conclude T1 is supported. If Group B’s average score is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A’s, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the test is inconclusive and further research is needed.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Homeowner Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a premium-priced home thermal management kit marketed as a safety/comfort upgrade for vehicles; Group B sees the same kit marketed as a proven automotive solution that integrates seamlessly with vehicles. Both groups are asked about willingness to pay (maximum price they would pay) and purchase intent (probability of buying).. Sample: 400 homeowners (200 per group) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region to reflect a representative sample of individual buyers.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (in euros) and purchase intent (percentage) for each group.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show at least 15% higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than Group B.; T2: Group B will show at least 15% higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than Group A.. Decision rule: If Group A’s average willingness to pay and purchase intent are at least 15% higher than Group B’s, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners (support T1). If Group B’s average willingness to pay and purchase intent are at least 15% higher than Group A’s, develop a consumer proposition focused on automotive integration (support T2). If neither difference meets the 15% threshold, do not invest in a consumer proposition and maintain the current B2B focus.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners that positions the product as a safety/comfort upgrade, supported by evidence of Eberspacher showcasing home thermal management at a trade show and the existence of a residential market for diesel heaters. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Compact vs Sustainable Home Brewing Kit" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase decision. Participants view two product concepts: (1) a compact, high-quality home brewing kit (Steinecker) positioned as reliable and space‑friendly; (2) a sustainable packaging kit (eco‑friendly capsules) positioned as environmentally responsible. Each concept includes a price premium (e.g., 20% above standard home brewing kit). Participants indicate likelihood to purchase and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 500 U.S. adults who have brewed beer at home in the past year, recruited via an online panel. Stratified by age and gender to reflect home brewing demographics.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and maximum price willingness to pay (continuous). Secondary measure: stated importance of compactness vs sustainability.. Predictions: T1: Participants will choose the compact kit and indicate higher willingness to pay for compactness than for sustainability.; T2: Participants will choose the sustainable kit and indicate higher willingness to pay for sustainability than for compactness.. Decision rule: If the compact kit achieves a purchase intent rate of at least 40% and a maximum price willingness to pay at least 20% above the sustainable kit, proceed to develop a differentiated compact consumer proposition. If the sustainable kit meets both thresholds, develop a differentiated sustainable consumer proposition. If neither meets thresholds, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 2000 euros, 4 weeks.

Test "Homeowner Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product descriptions and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 homeowners in target regions (e.g., Germany, Austria, Switzerland) who own a motorhome, RV, or car with auxiliary heaters.. Measure: Average WTP in euros for a home unit compared to a standard 12V heater, and self-reported primary motivation (safety/comfort vs. weight/fuel efficiency).. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP for the home unit than for the 12V heater, and motivation will be safety/comfort.; T2: Higher average WTP for the home unit that emphasizes weight savings/fuel efficiency than for the 12V heater, and motivation will be performance.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the home unit exceeds the WTP for the 12V heater by at least 20% and the primary motivation is safety/comfort, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20% or the primary motivation is weight/fuel efficiency, do not invest in a consumer proposition.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners, focusing on safety and comfort benefits. Begin with a targeted online survey (as proposed in test X1) to validate willingness to pay and primary motivation before committing to product development. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners, focusing on safety and comfort benefits. Begin with a targeted online survey (as proposed in test X1) to validate willingness to pay and primary motivation before committing to product development. Target customer: Homeowners who own motorhomes, RVs, or vehicles with auxiliary heaters in regions with extreme weather conditions where vehicle auxiliary heaters are insufficient.. Value proposition: A dedicated Eberspacher home unit that delivers reliable, consistent heating performance and safety, addressing the gap left by vehicle auxiliary heaters.. Favoured theory: T1. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Personal Enjoyment vs Functional Need" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A (personal enjoyment) and Group B (functional need). Each group views a product description of a Rieter-inspired spinning machine and is asked to indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) and likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale.. Sample: 300 respondents: 150 per group, recruited via craft and hobby forums to ensure self-identified crafters and small-scale producers.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (EUR) and purchase intent (1‑2 scale) for each group.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group B, indicating purchase driven by personal enjoyment.; T2: Group B will show higher average WTP and purchase intent than Group A, indicating purchase driven by functional need.. Decision rule: If Group A’s average WTP is at least 20% higher than Group B’s, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on personal enjoyment. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Digital Refund vs Reward Test" between T1; T2. Method: Randomized controlled trial with two arms: Arm A receives a digital refund via a mobile app; Arm B receives a tangible reward (e.g., a discount or loyalty point) for recycling. Participants are recruited from a retail location and asked to return beverage containers. The test runs for 4 weeks, with participants in each arm receiving a separate message about the reward mechanism.. Sample: 200 households (100 per arm) recruited from a single retail location in a mid-sized city, ensuring diversity in age, gender, and income.. Measure: Primary measure: number of containers returned per participant per week. Secondary measures: self-reported reason for returning (convenience vs reward) and willingness to pay a small fee for the reward.. Predictions: T1: Arm A will show at least 20% higher return rates than Arm B, and participants will cite convenience as the primary reason.; T2: Arm B will show at least 15% higher return rates than Arm A, and participants will cite the reward as the primary reason.. Decision rule: If Arm A return rate exceeds Arm B by at least 20 percentage points, conclude T1 is supported. If Arm B return rate exceeds Arm A by at least 15 percentage points, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 15 percentage points, both theories remain plausible and further testing is needed.. Cost: 18000 euros, 4 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.. Sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.; T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.. Decision rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Private electric car owners will purchase Lapp’s charging accessories if they perceive a clear convenience advantage (e.g., easy installation, fast charging, or integration with smart home systems) that reduces charging friction compared to competitors. Who benefits: Lapp Mobility GmbH benefits by capturing higher-margin sales directly to consumers and by building brand awareness in the consumer market.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view charging as a friction point and Lapp offers a solution that eliminates or reduces that friction, they will switch from generic accessories to Lapp, driven by perceived convenience and reliability.. How value is captured: Lapp would sell premium-priced charging kits directly to consumers through its own e-commerce or retail channels, earning higher margins than bulk B2B sales.. Assumptions: Consumers currently find charging accessories cumbersome and are price-sensitive.; Lapp can design a product that significantly reduces installation time or provides a unique convenience feature.; Lapp’s existing distribution network can reach private buyers without major changes.. T2: Private electric car owners will purchase Lapp’s charging accessories if they receive incentives or subsidies from governments or utility providers that lower the effective price, making the product affordable and attractive. Who benefits: Lapp Mobility GmbH benefits by capturing sales that would otherwise be delayed or blocked by price sensitivity, and by building relationships with incentivizing entities that could lead to future contracts.. Why behaviour changes: If a subsidy or incentive removes the price barrier, consumers will choose Lapp even if they perceive no additional convenience, because the cost is reduced.. Favours T1: Run the proposed Convenience vs Incentive Messaging Test (X1) to measure purchase intent under convenience and incentive messaging. Target customer: Private electric car owners who install charging accessories at home.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Premium vs Professional-Grade Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a Gühring drill bit marketed as either (A) premium, high‑performance metalworking tool for hobbyists/small workshops (T1) or (B) professional‑grade tool for demanding projects (T2). They are asked about willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale and purchase intent (1‑10).. Sample: 200 participants: 100 self‑identified hobbyists/small workshop owners (recruited via metalworking forums and social media) and 100 professionals (recruited via industry associations and LinkedIn). Randomly assign each participant to one of two message versions.. Measure: Average WTP (EUR) and average purchase intent score for each message version.. Predictions: T1: Hobbyists exposed to premium messaging will show a higher average WTP and purchase intent than those exposed to professional messaging.; T2: Professionals exposed to professional messaging will show a higher average WTP and purchase intent than those exposed to premium messaging.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for premium messaging exceeds professional messaging by at least 15% (or purchase intent by at least 10 points on the 1‑10 scale) among hobbyists, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. If the opposite holds for professionals, proceed to develop a professional‑grade consumer proposition. If neither. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.
