T1: Individual homeowners and small businesses will adopt automated storage systems if they perceive a clear, measurable benefit that directly reduces their storage costs or improves space utilization, because they are price-sensitive and value tangible returns on investment. Who benefits: Homeowners and small business owners who currently store items manually and incur high storage costs or limited space.. Why behaviour changes: They would change from manual storage to automated storage if they can demonstrate a cost savings or space efficiency that is quantifiable and easy to understand, such as reduced rental costs or increased usable space.. How value is captured: Kardex would capture value by selling a differentiated consumer product (e.g., a compact, affordable vertical lift module) and offering a subscription or service model for maintenance and performance monitoring.. Assumptions: There is a measurable cost savings or space efficiency that can be communicated to consumers.; Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that directly reduces their storage costs.; Kardex can produce or license a product that meets consumer expectations for size, safety, and ease of use.. Predictions: In a test offering a consumer product with a clear cost-saving claim, purchase intent or pre-orders will be higher than a control offering a generic B2B product.; Surveyed consumers will rank cost savings as the top reason for purchasing, with a higher willingness to pay for a product that promises a measurable return on investment..

T2: Individual homeowners and small businesses will adopt automated storage systems if they perceive a lifestyle or convenience benefit that aligns with modern living patterns, such as easy access to stored items, reduced clutter, or integration with smart home ecosystems, because they value convenience and status. Who benefits: Homeowners and small business owners who prioritize convenience, organization, and modern living.. Why behaviour changes: They would change from manual storage to automated storage if the system offers features like remote access, automated retrieval, or seamless integration with smart devices, making storage feel like a modern convenience rather than a cost.. How value is captured: Kardex would capture value by positioning a consumer product as a lifestyle upgrade, offering premium features (e.g., touchscreen interfaces, app integration) and potentially a subscription for software updates and support.. Assumptions: Consumers associate automated storage with modern convenience and status.; Smart home integration is a meaningful differentiator for this segment.; Kardex can develop or license features that meet these lifestyle expectations without major product redesign.. Predictions: In a test offering a lifestyle-focused product, purchase intent will be higher than a control offering a functional B2B product.; Surveyed consumers will rank convenience and status as the top reasons for purchasing, with a higher willingness to pay for a product that feels like a modern convenience..

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Cost Savings vs. Convenience" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a cost-saving proposition (e.g., 'Save EUR 200/year on storage costs with our compact vertical lift module') and a functional description of the product. Group B sees a convenience proposition (e.g., 'Easy access to stored items with remote control and app integration'). Both groups see the same product details and a call to pre-order or purchase.. Sample: 500 adults aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and geographic region to ensure representativeness.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: pre-order or purchase) and willingness to pay (maximum amount willing to pay).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B, because the cost-saving message directly addresses a measurable financial benefit.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A, because the convenience message aligns with modern living patterns and status.. Decision rule: If Group A's purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group B's, conclude T1 is more supported. If Group B's purchase intent is at least 15 percentage points higher than Group A, conclude T2 is more supported. If the difference is below 15 percentage points, both theories remain equally supported and further testing is needed.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes measurable cost savings and space efficiency, targeting homeowners and small businesses. T1: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine (RVM) for residential deposit return if they perceive a convenient, digital refund mechanism that is easy to use and accessible via a mobile app, because convenience and digital payout reduce friction and increase willingness to return containers. Who benefits: Individual consumers who receive digital refunds and can return containers from home, and retailers who gain foot traffic and can brand themselves as eco‑friendly.. Why behaviour changes: Convenience (no need to visit a redemption center) and digital refund (instant payout without cash) lower perceived effort and reduce barriers to participation.. How value is captured: TOMRA can charge a subscription fee for the app and service, or earn revenue from data on consumer return habits that can be sold to retailers or recycling programs.. Assumptions: Consumers trust the app to accurately track returns and provide refunds.; Retailers are willing to partner with TOMRA to offer the service and promote it to customers.; Regulatory frameworks in target markets permit digital refund mechanisms for deposit return.. Predictions: In a test offering the app to a residential building, at least 30% of residents will register and return containers within the first month.; Surveyed satisfaction with the digital refund process will be rated “very satisfied” by at least 70% of users.; Retailers will report increased foot traffic and repeat purchases among customers who use the app for bottle returns..

T2: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine (RVM) for residential deposit return if they receive a tangible cash refund (e.g., a voucher or coin return) that is easily redeemable at nearby retailers, because physical money provides immediate gratification and reduces trust concerns about digital refunds. Who benefits: Individual consumers who receive cash refunds and can redeem them for goods or services, and retailers who gain additional foot traffic and can partner to facilitate redemption.. Why behaviour changes: Physical cash eliminates the need for a digital refund mechanism and associated trust in app accuracy, making the return process more tangible and convenient for consumers.. How value is captured: TOMRA can charge a subscription fee for the cash‑return service, or earn revenue from retailer partnerships that share redemption revenue.. Assumptions: Consumers prefer physical cash refunds over digital refunds for deposit returns.; Retailers are willing to accept and redeem consumer‑generated RVM returns as a marketing incentive.; Regulatory frameworks permit cash refunds for consumer‑generated deposits.. Predictions: In a test offering cash refunds via a vending machine, at least 25% of participating households will redeem at least one refund within two weeks.; Surveyed satisfaction with cash refund will be rated “very satisfied” by at least 60% of users.; Retailers will report a measurable increase in purchases from customers who use the cash‑return service..

Test "Digital vs Cash Refund Consumer Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups in a residential building (e.g., apartment complex). Group A receives a digital refund via the myTOMRA app; Group B receives a tangible cash refund (e.g., voucher or coin return) via a vending machine. Both groups have access to the same sensor-based sorting bin and can return containers at any time. The test runs for 12 weeks, with weekly. Sample: 200 households (100 per group) in a building with a high density of residents who shop at nearby retailers.. Measure: 1) Number of containers returned per household per week (digital refund group vs cash refund group). 2) Self-reported satisfaction with refund process (digital vs cash) on a 1‑10 scale. 3) Retailer foot traffic data (if available) for stores located near the building.. Predictions: T1: Group A (digital refund) will have at least 30% higher return rates than Group B (cash refund) and higher satisfaction ratings, because convenience and digital payout reduce friction.; T2: Group B (cash refund) will have at least 30% higher return rates than Group A (digital refund) and higher satisfaction ratings, because physical cash provides immediate gratification and reduces trust concerns.. Decision rule: If Group A’s return rate exceeds Group B’s by at least 15 percentage points (e.g., 35% vs 20%) and Group A’s satisfaction score is at least 2 points higher than Group B’s, then T1 is supported. If Group B’s return rate exceeds Group A’s by at least 15 percentage points and Group B’s satisfaction score is at least 2 points higher, then T2 is supported. If neither. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Home brewers will purchase Krones equipment directly if they perceive it as a premium, reliable brand that reduces setup complexity and offers scalable production. Who benefits: Home brewers seeking high-quality, easy-to-use equipment that can grow with their hobby.. Why behaviour changes: If brewers view Krones as a trusted brand that simplifies scaling from hobby to commercial, they will be willing to buy directly rather than relying on distributors or competitors.. How value is captured: Krones captures value through premium pricing, direct-to-consumer sales, and reduced distribution costs, leveraging its existing brand reputation in the craft brewing segment.. Assumptions: Home brewers are willing to pay a premium for brand trust and reliability.; Krones can communicate scalability and ease of use effectively to home brewers.; Direct sales channel is feasible and cost-effective for Krones.. Predictions: A test offering a Krones home brewing kit at a premium price directly to home brewers will achieve a purchase rate of at least 15% of those exposed.; Surveyed intent to buy will be higher for Krones than for a generic competitor offering similar functionality..

T2: Home brewers will purchase Krones equipment directly if they can access it through a subscription or rental model that lowers upfront cost and provides ongoing support, because they value flexibility and risk mitigation. Who benefits: Home brewers with limited capital who want to try commercial brewing without a large investment.. Why behaviour changes: If brewers can rent or subscribe to Krones equipment, they avoid the need for a large purchase and gain access to professional-grade technology, reducing perceived risk and enabling experimentation.. How value is captured: Krones captures value through recurring revenue from subscriptions, reduced customer acquisition costs, and data on usage patterns that can inform product improvements.. Assumptions: Home brewers are price-sensitive and prefer lower upfront cost.; A subscription model can be integrated with Krones’ existing technology and service infrastructure.; Brewers will commit to a subscription if they perceive value in flexibility and support.. Predictions: A test offering a subscription-based Krones home brewing kit will achieve a subscription uptake rate of at least 10% among targeted home brewers.; Surveyed intent to subscribe will be higher for Krones than for a generic competitor offering a similar subscription model..

Test "Direct-to-Consumer Purchase vs Subscription Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase and subscription offers. Participants are recruited from a panel of home brewers in Germany. They are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A receives a premium-priced direct-purchase offer for a Krones home brewing kit (e.g., €1,200). Group B receives a subscription offer for the same kit at a lower upfront cost (e.g., €800 upfront, €100/month for 12 months). Both offers include a. Sample: 200 home brewers (100 per group) who have purchased a home brewing kit in the past 12 months and are active on social media.. Measure: Purchase intent measured as a binary yes/no response to each offer. Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) for each offer.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent than Group B because home brewers value brand trust and are willing to pay a premium for a trusted premium brand.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent than Group A because home brewers prefer lower upfront cost and flexibility, and a subscription model reduces risk.. Decision rule: If Group A purchase intent ≥ 30% and Group B ≤ 20%, conclude T1 is better supported. If Group B purchase intent ≥ 30% and Group A ≤ 20%, conclude T2 is better supported. If both groups show ≥ 30% intent, the evidence is inconclusive and further testing is needed.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

If the test shows purchase intent above 30% for the premium offer, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting home brewers who value brand trust and are willing to pay a premium. case.question: Should Nabtesco Corporation develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing precision reduction gears, automatic doors, transport equipment and welfare components sold to manufacturers, building owners and transport operators? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Home Automation Product Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 300 homeowners (150 affluent, 150 moderate) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and home ownership.. Measure: 1) Purchase intent: binary (would buy) and WTP (maximum price). 2) Motivation ranking: self-reported primary reason for buying (convenience vs. status).. Predictions: T1: Affluent homeowners will show higher purchase intent and WTP for a convenience-focused kit than moderate homeowners, and will rank convenience as primary motivation.; T2: Affluent homeowners will show higher purchase intent and WTP for a status-focused kit than moderate homeowners, and will rank status as primary motivation.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the convenience kit among affluent homeowners exceeds €1,500 and is at least 20% higher than the WTP for the status kit, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition focused on convenience. If the average WTP for the status kit exceeds €2,000 and is at least 20% higher than the WTP for the convenience kit, develop a status-focused proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not invest.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Conduct the proposed Home Automation Product Preference Test (X1) to empirically distinguish between convenience and status motivations. If the test confirms that affluent homeowners show higher willingness to pay for a convenience-focused kit, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing convenience. If the test shows no significant difference or the status kit outperforms, reconsider the B2B Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Eberspächer Gruppe GmbH & Co. KG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing exhaust technology, vehicle heaters and thermal management systems for vehicle manufacturers and specialist dealers? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Sample: 500 homeowners in target regions (e.g., Germany, Austria, Switzerland) who own a motorhome, RV, or car with auxiliary heaters.. Measure: Average WTP in euros for a home unit compared to a standard 12V heater, and self-reported primary motivation (safety/comfort vs. weight/fuel efficiency).. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP for the home unit than for the 12V heater, and motivation will be safety/comfort.; T2: Higher average WTP for the home unit that emphasizes weight savings/fuel efficiency than for the 12V heater, and motivation will be performance.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the home unit exceeds the WTP for the 12V heater by at least 20% and the primary motivation is safety/comfort, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 20% or the primary motivation is weight/fuel efficiency, do not invest in a consumer proposition.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners, focusing on safety and comfort benefits. Begin with a targeted online survey (as proposed in test X1) to validate willingness to pay and primary motivation before committing to product development. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: The simulated parking-heater offer test (SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE) does not provide evidence that homeowners are aware of Eberspacher or willing to pay a premium for home units; it only tests installation friction. Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners, focusing on safety and comfort benefits. Target customer: Homeowners who own motorhomes, RVs, or car auxiliary heaters in regions with extreme weather conditions where vehicle auxiliary heaters are insufficient.. Value proposition: A dedicated Eberspacher home unit that delivers reliable, consistent heating performance and safety, addressing the gap left by vehicle auxiliary heaters.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Homeowner Preference Test (500 homeowners, €15,000, 8 weeks) to measure willingness to pay and primary motivation before any product development.. Uncertainty: The test will determine whether homeowners are aware of Eberspacher and willing to pay a premium for home units. If the test shows a willingness-to-pay gap of less than 20% or the primary motivation is weight/fuel efficiency, the investment. Would change if: The test shows a willingness-to-pay gap of at least 20% and the primary motivation is safety/comfort, indicating strong consumer demand for a differentiated home unit.; Evidence emerges that homeowners are aware of Eberspacher and actively seek premium-priced home units, supporting T2.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Test "Consumer vs Professional Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from two distinct segments: homeowners in cold climates and professional users (camping, motorhomes, commercial vehicles). Each segment receives one of two product descriptions: (1) safety and comfort-focused (homeowners) or (2) durability and performance-focused (professional users). After viewing the description, participants indicate willingness to pay a premium (20% above comparable competitors) and intent to purchase.. Sample: 500 participants: 250 homeowners (cold climates) and 250 professional users (outdoor/commercial). Recruit via targeted online panels to ensure geographic and demographic representation.. Measure: Willingness to pay premium (percentage of participants offering a price 20% above comparable competitors) and purchase intent (binary: "Would purchase this product").. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will show higher willingness to pay premium and higher purchase intent than professional users.; T2: Professional users will show higher willingness to pay premium and higher purchase intent than homeowners.. Decision rule: If homeowners' willingness to pay premium exceeds professional users' willingness to pay by at least 5 percentage points, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners. If professional users' willingness to pay exceeds homeowners' by at least 5 percentage points, pursue a professional-focused proposition. If the difference is below 5 percentage points, no expansion is recommended.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Each group sees one of two product descriptions: (A) a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing sustainability, quality, and home use; (B) a small‑producer proposition emphasizing yield improvement, cost savings, and supply‑chain independence. Both descriptions include a price point and a call to action to purchase a Rieter spinning machine. Participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay.. Sample: 400 participants (200 hobbyists, 200 small producers) from the US and EU, recruited via online panels.. Measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willingness to pay for each product description.. Predictions: T1: Hobbyists will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the consumer proposition than small producers.; T2: Small producers will show higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay for the small‑producer proposition than hobbyists.. Decision rule: If the consumer proposition achieves at least 30% purchase intent among hobbyists and at least 20% among small producers, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the small‑producer proposition achieves at least 30% purchase intent among small producers and at least 20% among hobbyists, proceed to develop a small‑producer focused proposition. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into consumer or small‑producer markets.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., home‑use filling kit for small brewers).; 2) Expand B2B offerings by adding consumer‑focused features to existing machines (e.g., smart packaging sensors).; 3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on B2B beverage and liquid‑food producers.; 4) Partner with consumer brands to co‑develop a branded filling/packaging solution rather than selling under Krones brand.; 5) Target a new consumer segment with a different value proposition (e.g., eco‑friendly packaging for health‑conscious consumers)..

T1: Small brewers and home brewers will adopt Krones equipment because they need compact, reliable machines that fit tight spaces and produce consistent results, and Krones can capture value by selling premium, high-quality machines at a margin. Who benefits: Small brewers and home brewers gain access to professional-grade equipment that meets their space and output needs.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently lack suitable equipment for small-batch or home brewing; a compact, reliable machine reduces setup time and improves consistency, making it a necessary purchase.. How value is captured: Krones sells higher-margin compact machines directly to these users, leveraging its existing engineering and brand credibility.. Assumptions: Small brewers and home brewers are willing to pay a premium for compact equipment.; Krones can adapt its existing compact-class technology to meet consumer needs without major redesign.; Distribution channels exist for direct-to-consumer sales of compact machines.. Predictions: A survey of small brewers will show >50% would purchase a compact Krones machine if priced at $3,000-$5,000.; Sales of compact machines will increase in regions with high craft brewery growth (e.g., U.S., Germany)..

T2: Home brewers will adopt Krones equipment because they seek convenience and convenience-driven packaging solutions that reduce preparation time and waste, and Krones can capture value by offering integrated, branded packaging systems that simplify the brewing process. Who benefits: Home brewers gain a time-saving, waste-reducing brewing experience; Krones gains a new revenue stream through branded packaging integration.. Why behaviour changes: Home brewers currently spend time and effort on manual packaging and brewing; a turnkey, integrated system reduces effort and improves consistency, making it an attractive purchase.. How value is captured: Krones sells integrated packaging systems as part of a home brewing kit, leveraging its existing packaging technology and brand to command premium pricing.. Assumptions: Home brewers are willing to pay for a turnkey, integrated system that reduces manual work.; Krones can adapt its packaging technology to consumer-scale production without major redesign.; Distribution channels exist for selling integrated kits directly to consumers.. Predictions: A survey of home brewers will show >40% would purchase a turnkey brewing kit if priced at $2,500-$4,000.; Sales of integrated packaging kits will increase in regions with high home brewing adoption (e.g., U.S., Germany)..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Compact vs Integrated Home Brewing Kits" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase decisions. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a compact machine description (T1) or an integrated packaging system description (T2). They are then asked to indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) in a 7-point scale and to state a purchase intent (yes/no).. Sample: 500 U.S. adults who have brewed beer at home in the past year, recruited via an online panel. Stratify by age (18-35, 36-55, 56+).. Measure: Average WTP (in euros) and purchase intent (percentage) for each condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent for the compact machine description than for the integrated packaging system.; T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent for the integrated packaging system description than for the compact machine description.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the compact machine is at least 20% higher than the average WTP for the integrated packaging system, conclude T1 is more likely. If the average WTP for the integrated packaging system is at least 20% higher than the average WTP for the compact machine, conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is less than 20% points, the test is inconclusive and further data is needed.. Cost: 1500 euros, 2 weeks.

case.question: Should Sika AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing construction chemicals, sealants and adhesives for contractors, distributors and industrial manufacturers? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable sealants, adhesives, or waterproofing for home improvement.. Why behaviour changes: If Sika can communicate that its products are designed for everyday use, are easy to apply, and deliver professional outcomes, consumers will shift from generic store‑brand sealants to Sika, reducing reliance on contractor‑only solutions.. How value is captured: Sika would capture value through higher retail margins on consumer‑branded items, direct‑to‑consumer sales, and brand extension into home improvement retail.. Assumptions: Consumers trust Sika’s professional reputation and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.; Retail distribution (e.g., hardware stores, online marketplaces) is accessible and cost‑effective for Sika.; Marketing can effectively communicate ease‑of‑use and professional results to DIY buyers.. Predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded DIY sealant at a price comparable to leading store‑brand sealants will achieve higher unit sales and repeat purchase rate among DIY shoppers compared to an identical product sold under a generic brand.; Surveyed DIY consumers will rate Sika’s product as “very easy to use” or “easy to use” at least 60% of the time, indicating perceived ease‑of‑application..

T2: Contractors will purchase Sika’s consumer products for residential projects because they need reliable, code‑compliant sealants and adhesives that can be used on both professional and personal jobs, reducing the need for separate supplier relationships. Who benefits: Contractors who work on both residential and commercial projects and value a single supplier for code‑compliant materials.. Why behaviour changes: If Sika offers a consumer‑branded line that meets residential building codes and is compatible with professional‑grade products, contractors can buy a single brand for both types of work, simplifying procurement and reducing inventory costs. How value is captured: Sika would capture value through higher volume sales to contractors, cross‑selling of professional and consumer lines, and reduced distribution costs by serving both B2B and B2C channels.. Assumptions: Contractors are willing to pay a premium for a single brand that meets both professional and residential standards.; Sika can produce consumer‑grade products that meet residential building codes without compromising professional performance.; Contractors are willing to purchase from Sika directly or through existing distribution channels.. Predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded sealant marketed as “professional‑grade for residential use” will achieve higher purchase intent among contractors compared to a generic store‑brand sealant marketed only for residential use.; Surveyed contractors will indicate that they would use Sika’s consumer product for at least 30% of their residential projects, citing code compliance and convenience..

case.question: Should Gühring KG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing precision rotary cutting tools for industrial metal machining? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Predictions: If marketed as a premium brand, Gühring will achieve at least 3% market share among hobbyists within 12 months, with average price paid 20% above generic alternatives.; Surveyed hobbyists will rank brand status as the top purchase driver for 40% of buyers..

Test "Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 200 hobbyists (100 per arm) via metalworking forums and social media. Randomly assign each participant to one of two conditions: Condition A: offer a Gühring drill at a 20% premium price (e.g., €120 instead of €100) with a brief description of precision and durability benefits. Condition B: offer the same drill at the same €100 price with no premium positioning, using the existing B2B online shop’s. Sample: 200 hobbyists (100 per arm). Measure: Purchase intent: binary “Would you buy this drill?” and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale.. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show at least 60% purchase intent and a WTP of at least €110, indicating hobbyists value premium positioning.; T2: Condition B will show at least 60% purchase intent and a WTP of at least €100, indicating they already purchase through B2B channels and price is secondary.. Decision rule: If purchase intent in Condition A ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €110, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition (supports T1). If purchase intent in Condition B ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €100, proceed with expanding B2B channels (supports T2). If neither condition meets thresholds, no expansion is. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a 20% premium-priced Gühring drill. If the test meets the thresholds (purchase intent ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €110), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition; otherwise, focus on expanding B2B channels or maintaining the current B2B-only model. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Run the proposed Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a 20% premium-priced Gühring drill. If the test meets the thresholds (purchase intent ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €110), proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition; otherwise, focus on expanding B2B channels or maintaining the current B2B-only model. Target customer: Individual hobbyists and small workshops (1‑10 employees) who need precision metalworking tools for personal or small‑scale projects.. Value proposition: A premium‑priced Gühring drill that delivers superior accuracy, durability, and brand reputation, sold directly to consumers via an online channel, leveraging existing B2B shop integration.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test (X1) within the 12‑week budget, targeting 200 hobbyists (100 per arm) via metalworking forums and social media.. Uncertainty: The size of the hobbyist market for Gühring tools, willingness to pay a premium, and whether hobbyists already obtain tools through B2B channels are unknown. The test will resolve these uncertainties.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent below 60% or WTP below €110, the favoured theory would shift to T2 and the recommendation would be to expand B2B channels.; If additional evidence shows hobbyists already purchase Gühring tools through B2B channels at high volumes, T2 would become more likely and the recommendation would shift accordingly.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Rieter Holding AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing short-staple spinning machines, components and after-sales services for industrial spinning mills? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Affordable CNC Machines" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view two product descriptions: a premium Biesse consumer CNC machine (high accuracy, professional-grade, €2,500 price) and an affordable Biesse consumer CNC machine (same accuracy, €1,200 price). They are asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale and purchase intent (1‑10).. Sample: 300 DIY woodworkers and homeowners recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and self‑reported experience with CNC machines.. Measure: Average WTP difference between premium and affordable versions (points). Purchase intent difference (points).. Predictions: T1: Premium version WTP ≥ 15% above affordable version; purchase intent for premium version ≥ 10% higher.; T2: Affordable version WTP ≥ 15% below premium version; purchase intent for affordable version ≥ 10% higher.. Decision rule: If premium WTP ≥ 15% above affordable WTP, proceed with premium consumer proposition. If affordable WTP ≥ 15% below premium WTP, proceed with affordable volume proposition. If neither condition met, no expansion recommended.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Low-Cost vs Subscription Model" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a consumer-branded, low-cost vertical lift module priced at $5,000 with a one-time purchase option. Group B sees the same module with a $1,000 monthly subscription for maintenance, upgrades, and support. Both groups are shown a brief description of the system and its benefits. The survey asks about purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay a premium (e.g., $100).. Sample: 300 small businesses and individual homeowners (100 per group), recruited via an online panel to match demographic criteria for small buyers.. Measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay a premium (e.g., $100).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Group B, because the low upfront cost is the primary barrier.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Group A, because the subscription model reduces the perceived cost of ownership.. Decision rule: If Group A purchase intent is at least 30% and Group B is at least 25%, proceed with the low-cost one-time purchase model. If Group B purchase intent is at least 30% and Group A is at least 25%, proceed with the subscription model. If neither threshold is met, do not expand into a consumer proposition and continue focusing on B2B.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Consumers will adopt a direct‑to‑consumer reverse vending machine (RVM) for deposit refund if they receive a convenient digital payout and clear navigation to drop‑off locations. Who benefits: Consumers seeking refund for empty containers; TOMRA via higher transaction volume and data on consumer behavior.. Why behaviour changes: Current consumer experience involves visiting retail or return centers; a digital refund and drop‑off convenience reduces friction and makes return more attractive.. How value is captured: TOMRA captures value by monetizing each transaction with a small margin (e.g., refund processing fee) and by selling data on consumer recycling patterns to retailers or deposit systems.. T2: Consumers will adopt a direct‑to‑consumer reverse vending machine (RVM) for deposit refund if they receive a tangible reward (e.g., points, discounts) that can be redeemed at nearby retailers, making the return experience more valuable. Who benefits: Consumers seeking immediate value for their containers; TOMRA via higher transaction frequency and potential retailer partnerships.. Why behaviour changes: Current consumer experience involves visiting retail or return centers; a tangible reward links return to a specific retailer, creating a clear incentive to drop‑off and increasing the perceived value of the refund.. How value is captured: TOMRA captures value by earning a small margin on each transaction and by selling data on consumer redemption patterns to retailers, who may increase shelf space for deposit‑ready products.. Assumptions: Consumers value immediate rewards over digital refunds alone.; Retailers are willing to partner to offer rewards that drive foot traffic.; Regulatory frameworks permit retailer‑linked refund mechanisms.. Predictions: In a pilot with a consumer RVM offering retailer‑linked points, return rates will be at least 10% higher than baseline RVMs in comparable locations.; Consumers will redeem rewards at the offering retailer at a rate at least 15% higher than baseline redemption rates for existing RVMs..

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

case.question: Should U.I. Lapp GmbH develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing cables and connection technology for industrial machinery and plant engineering? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. Why behaviour changes: Current deposit refund systems often require physical travel to redemption centers, which consumers find inconvenient. Test "Digital Refund vs Public Placement Choice Experiment" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with randomized exposure to digital refund/map proposition (T1) or public placement/digital refund proposition (T2). Participants view a mock consumer reverse vending machine and are asked to indicate whether they would use it and, if yes, whether they would prefer a digital refund or a physical refund. They also rate perceived convenience and likelihood to visit a public location.. Sample: 500 Norwegian consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who select "Would use" for each proposition. Secondary outcomes: (a) preference for digital vs physical refund (binary); (b) perceived convenience (1‑10 scale); (c) likelihood to visit a public location (1‑10 scale).. Predictions: T1: Proportion who select "Would use" for digital refund proposition will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for public placement proposition.; T2: Proportion who select "Would use" for public placement proposition will be at least 15 percentage points higher than for digital refund proposition.. Decision rule: If the observed difference between the two proportions is ≥ 15 percentage points in favor of the digital refund proposition, conclude T1 is better supported. If the difference is ≥ 15 percentage points in favor of the public placement proposition, conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is <15 pp, both theories remain. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.. Sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.; T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.. Decision rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus. Target customer: German EV owners planning home charging within 12 months who value automotive-grade performance and are willing to pay a premium for reliability.. Next action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within 12 weeks, targeting 300 German EV owners, to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the premium and specialized concepts.. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence that consumers will adopt a premium proposition or that compatibility is the primary purchase driver. Would change if: If the test shows premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the premium proposition (supporting T1).; If the test shows specialized intent ≥ 45% and premium intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the specialized proposition (supporting T2).; If neither meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend no expansion.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Direct-to-Consumer Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are recruited from a panel of home brewers and craft brewers. They are randomly assigned to one of two scenarios: (A) Premium direct-purchase offering with a fixed price and clear brand positioning; (B) Subscription model with low upfront cost and recurring service. Both scenarios include a product description, price, and a brief explanation of the brand’s reliability and yield benefits. Participants indicate whether they would purchase (. Sample: 200 home brewers and 200 craft brewers, recruited via a panel that matches demographic and geographic distribution of the target market.. Measure: Purchase intent measured as a binary “Would you buy this product?” (yes/no) and willingness to pay (WTP) measured as a maximum price they would pay.. Predictions: T1: In scenario A, purchase intent will be higher among home brewers than among craft brewers, and average WTP will be at least 15% above comparable competitors.; T2: In scenario B, purchase intent will be higher among home brewers than among craft brewers, and monthly subscription revenue per user will be at least 10% lower than a comparable direct purchase offering.. Decision rule: If purchase intent in scenario A exceeds that in scenario B by at least 10 percentage points among home brewers, we conclude T1 is better supported. If purchase intent in scenario B exceeds that in scenario A by at least 10 percentage points among home brewers, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Test "Premium vs Community Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group B sees community messaging emphasizing collaboration, shared learning, and a makerspace experience. Both groups view a mock Biesse desktop CNC machine description and are asked to indicate willingness to pay a premium (20% above baseline price) and likelihood to purchase.. Sample: 300 individual woodworkers and hobbyists recruited via online panels, balanced across the two groups (150 per group).. Measure: Willingness to pay a premium (percentage willing to pay at least 20% more) and purchase intent (binary: would purchase).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than Group B.; T2: Group B will show higher willingness to pay and purchase intent than Group A.. Decision rule: If Group A’s willingness to pay premium exceeds Group B by at least 5 percentage points, adopt T1. If Group B’s willingness to pay premium exceeds Group A by at least 5 percentage points, adopt T2. If the difference is ≥ 5 percentage points, proceed with the corresponding differentiated proposition. If the difference is ≤ 5 percentage points, consider no expansion.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Test "Consumer vs Industrial Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a consumer-focused message emphasizing reduced manual labor and higher yield for hobbyists. Group B sees an industrial-focused message emphasizing scalability and modularity for small-scale producers. Both groups are presented with a product description of a compact spinning machine priced at €1,500 (T1) or €3,000 (T2). Participants indicate their likelihood to purchase on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 hobbyists (self-identified crafters) and 250 small-scale producers (fewer than 20 animals, less than 50 pounds of fiber). Recruited via online panels to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely"). Secondary measure: stated willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group B, indicating demand for a consumer proposition.; T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Group A, indicating demand for an industrial proposition.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for Group A is at least 1.5 points higher than Group B and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), conclude T1 is supported. If Group B’s average purchase intent is at least 1.5 points higher than Group A and the difference is statistically significant, conclude T2 is supported. If neither difference meets the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

Test "Consumer Messaging Test: Safety vs Prestige" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants view two product descriptions of the same LAPP consumer cable (e.g., home networking cable) with identical price points. One description emphasizes safety and certification (e.g., "Certified for home networking, ETL‑certified, ETL‑tested for safety"), while the other emphasizes prestige and status (e.g., "Premium‑grade cable with industrial‑grade durability, designed for the discerning consumer"). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑not interested to 7‑very interested).. Sample: 500 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect a broad consumer base.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑to 7) for each messaging condition.. Predictions: T1: Safety‑certified messaging will generate purchase intent at least 15% higher than prestige messaging.; T2: Prestige‑positioned messaging will generate purchase intent at least 15% higher than safety‑certified messaging.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between safety‑certified and prestige messaging is ≥ 15 points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition based on the winning messaging. If the difference is ≤ 15 points, conclude insufficient evidence to justify investment and recommend no expansion.. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.. Sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.; T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.. Decision rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

T1: Individual consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive a clear, direct financial benefit (deposit refunds) and a convenient digital experience, because they value immediate financial reward and simplicity over traditional collection methods. Who benefits: Households with single-use containers who currently drop off containers at bag-drops or redemption centers.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers are motivated by the tangible return of their deposit and the convenience of a digital app, which reduces the effort of finding a collection point and waiting for a refund.. How value is captured: TOMRA captures value through a subscription or transaction fee for the digital payout service, plus potential data monetization from recycling behavior insights.. Assumptions: Consumers currently use bag-drops or redemption centers for deposit returns.; A digital payout system can be integrated without major retailer infrastructure changes.; Consumers are willing to pay a small fee for the digital service.. Predictions: In a test offering a digital payout app with a refund threshold of €5, at least 30% of targeted households will complete a deposit return transaction within 12 weeks.; User retention rate for the app will be above 20% after 12 weeks, indicating continued usage beyond the initial refund..

T2: Individual consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they view recycling as an environmental responsibility and are motivated by the collective impact of their actions, because they seek to contribute to sustainability and reduce waste. Who benefits: Environmentally conscious households that already recycle but seek a more visible, community-driven way to do so.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers are motivated by the belief that their individual actions contribute to a larger environmental goal, creating a sense of purpose and community involvement.. How value is captured: TOMRA captures value through a subscription or participation fee that funds environmental initiatives, plus potential brand association with sustainability.. Assumptions: Consumers currently recycle but lack a mechanism to track their impact.; A community-driven platform can be built without requiring retailer or government involvement.; Consumers are willing to pay a fee for the environmental impact tracking service.. Predictions: In a test offering a community impact tracking app with a participation fee of €2 per month, at least 25% of targeted households will sign up within 12 weeks.; User engagement (e.g., daily check-ins) will be above 15% after 12 weeks, indicating sustained participation beyond the initial fee..

Test "Digital Payout vs Environmental Tracking Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a digital payout app (financial reward) or an environmental impact tracking app (community-driven). Participants are recruited from households with single-use containers. Each arm offers a refund or participation fee, and a follow-up survey measures intent to adopt and willingness to pay.. Sample: 500 households (250 per arm) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and recycling frequency.. Measure: Primary outcome: percentage of households choosing the arm (digital payout vs environmental tracking) within 12 weeks. Secondary outcomes: willingness to pay (refund amount) and intent to adopt (binary).. Predictions: T1: Digital payout arm will achieve at least 30% choice rate and higher willingness to pay than environmental tracking arm.; T2: Environmental tracking arm will achieve at least 25% choice rate and higher willingness to pay than digital payout arm.. Decision rule: If digital payout arm choice rate ≥ 30% and its willingness to pay ≥ €5, proceed to develop a digital payout consumer proposition. If environmental tracking arm choice rate ≥ 25% and its willingness to pay ≥ €2, develop an environmental impact tracking proposition. If neither condition is met, do not expand.. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Proceed to develop a digital payout consumer proposition for individual households, as it is supported by evidence of TOMRA’s existing consumer app (myTOMRA) and the popularity of bag-drops. The test should measure choice rate and willingness to pay to validate demand before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Proceed to develop a digital payout consumer proposition for individual households, as it is supported by evidence of TOMRA’s existing consumer app (myTOMRA) and the popularity of bag-drops. The test should measure choice rate and willingness to pay to validate demand before scaling. Target customer: Households with single-use containers who currently use bag-drops or redemption centers for deposit returns.. Value proposition: A digital payout app that provides immediate deposit refunds and a map to nearby recycling points, making recycling more convenient and financially rewarding.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Digital Payout vs Environmental Tracking Test (500 households, 12 weeks, €18,000) to measure choice rate and willingness to pay. If the digital payout arm meets the 30% choice rate and €5 refund threshold, proceed to build. Uncertainty: The evidence does not show whether consumers are motivated by financial reward or environmental responsibility, nor does it quantify willingness to pay for a digital payout service. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows the environmental tracking arm achieving at least 25% choice rate and a willingness to pay of €2 per month, we would reconsider a community-driven proposition.; If the test fails to meet the choice rate or refund threshold, we would abandon expansion and focus on existing B2B markets.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Who benefits: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable sealants, adhesives, or waterproofing for home improvement.. Why behaviour changes: If Sika can communicate that its products are designed for everyday use, are easy to apply, and deliver professional outcomes, consumers will shift from generic store‑brand sealants to Sika, reducing reliance on contractor‑only solutions.. How value is captured: Sika would capture value through higher retail margins on consumer‑branded items, direct‑to‑consumer sales, and brand extension into home improvement retail.. Predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded DIY sealant at a price comparable to leading store‑brand sealants will achieve higher unit sales and repeat purchase rate among DIY shoppers compared to an identical product sold under a generic brand.; Surveyed DIY consumers will rate Sika’s product as “very easy to use” or “easy to use” at least 60% of the time, indicating perceived ease‑of‑application..

T2: Contractors will purchase Sika’s consumer products for residential projects because they need reliable, code‑compliant sealants and adhesives that can be used on both professional and personal jobs, reducing the need for separate supplier relationships. Who benefits: Contractors who work on both residential and commercial projects and value a single supplier for code‑compliant materials.. Why behaviour changes: If Sika offers a consumer‑branded line that meets residential building codes and is compatible with professional‑grade products, contractors can buy a single brand for both types of work, simplifying procurement and reducing inventory costs. How value is captured: Sika would capture value through higher volume sales to contractors, cross‑selling of professional and consumer lines, and reduced distribution costs by serving both B2B and B2C channels.. Assumptions: Contractors are willing to pay a premium for a single brand that meets both professional and residential standards.; Sika can produce consumer‑grade products that meet residential building codes without compromising professional performance.; Contractors are willing to purchase from Sika directly or through existing distribution channels.. Predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded sealant marketed as “professional‑grade for residential use” will achieve higher purchase intent among contractors compared to a generic store‑brand sealant marketed only for residential use.; Surveyed contractors will indicate that they would use Sika’s consumer product for at least 30% of their residential projects, citing code compliance and convenience..

Test "Consumer Purchase Intent Test: Sika vs Generic Store Brand" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a Sika-branded DIY sealant (highlighting ease-of-use, professional-grade results, and code compliance for residential use). Sample: 300 DIY consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and home improvement experience.. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage saying "Yes") for Sika-branded product versus generic store brand.. Predictions: T1: Sika-branded product will achieve a purchase intent rate at least 15 percentage points higher than the generic store brand.; T2: No significant difference in purchase intent between Sika-branded and generic store brand (difference <5 percentage points).. Decision rule: If Sika-branded purchase intent exceeds generic store brand by ≥15 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners. Test "Consumer Messaging Test for Assistive vs Lifestyle Home Automation" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of consumers with and without mobility impairments. Participants view a product description of a home automation device (e.g., a smart cane or posture support system) and are randomly assigned to one of two message conditions: (1) Medical necessity framing (emphasizing rehabilitation and mobility support) or (2) Lifestyle framing (emphasizing status, convenience, and modern living). After viewing the description, participants indicate their willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale and their purchase intent (1‑10).. Sample: 300 participants (150 with mobility impairments, 150 without) recruited via an online panel, balanced across both message conditions.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (WTP) and purchase intent (1‑10) for each message condition.. Predictions: T1: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the medical necessity condition compared to the lifestyle condition.; T2: Higher average WTP and purchase intent in the lifestyle condition compared to the medical necessity condition.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for the medical necessity condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the average WTP for the lifestyle condition, conclude T1 is supported. If the average WTP for the lifestyle condition is at least 1.5 points higher than the average WTP for the medical necessity condition, conclude T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, the results are inconclusive and further testing is recommended.. Cost: 15000 euros, 6 weeks.
