sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s precision tools if they perceive them as affordable, reliable, and compatible with existing CNC machines, because these attributes lower the perceived risk and cost of switching from other brands. Who benefits: Gühring benefits by capturing sales from a growing segment of individual buyers who value precision and compatibility, expanding its consumer market beyond B2B.. Why behaviour changes: If hobbyists view Gühring as a trusted, compatible alternative that performs as well as higher‑priced competitors, they will purchase it instead of cheaper alternatives or continue using existing tools.. How value is captured: Gühring can price its tools competitively while maintaining its premium reputation, generating revenue from a new consumer segment without diluting its brand in the industrial market.. Assumptions: Hobbyists and small workshops have sufficient discretionary budget for precision tools.; They are willing to invest in tools that promise reliable performance and compatibility with their existing CNC machines.; Gühring can produce tools at scale that meet hobbyist demand without compromising quality.. Predictions: If offered at a price 10‑20% below premium CNC tool brands, Gühring will achieve at least 5% market share among hobbyists within 12 months.; Customer surveys will show that compatibility with existing CNC machines is the top purchase driver for at least 60% of buyers..

T2: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s tools if they are marketed as premium, high‑performance products that demonstrate technical superiority and brand prestige, because status and perceived quality justify a higher price. Who benefits: Gühring benefits by commanding premium prices and expanding its brand into the consumer market, leveraging its industrial reputation to justify higher margins.. Why behaviour changes: If hobbyists perceive Gühring as a brand that offers unmatched precision and durability, they will choose it over cheaper alternatives even if the price is 20‑30% higher, because they value performance and brand prestige.. How value is captured: Gühring can price its tools at a premium while maintaining its industrial positioning, generating higher revenue per unit and potentially lower overall volume but still profitable.. Assumptions: Hobbyists are willing to pay a premium for perceived performance advantages.; They value brand prestige and technical differentiation.; Gühring can communicate these attributes effectively to individual buyers.. Predictions: If marketed as a premium brand, Gühring will achieve at least 3% market share among hobbyists within 12 months, even at a price 20‑30% above competitors.; Surveyed buyers will rank “brand prestige” as the top purchase driver for at least 40% of buyers..

Test "Hobbyist Price Sensitivity Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are recruited from hobbyist CNC forums (e.g., Tormach, CNCZone) and offered a Gühring drill bit at a price 10‑20% below its usual retail price (e.g., €150 instead of €180). They are asked to indicate whether they would purchase it and, if so, the maximum price they would pay. The test runs for 4 weeks, with 200 participants expected to complete the survey.. Sample: 200 hobbyists who have posted about CNC projects in the past 12 months, recruited via forum announcements and social media.. Measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: self‑reported importance of compatibility with existing CNC machines (1‑5 scale).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of participants will indicate purchase intent at the discounted price, and compatibility will be ranked as the top purchase driver for at least 60% of those who would buy.; T2: At least 30% of participants will indicate purchase intent at the discounted price, and brand prestige will be ranked as the top purchase driver for at least 40% of those who would buy.. Decision rule: If purchase intent ≥ 30% AND compatibility ranks ≥ 60% of purchase‑intent group, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing compatibility. If purchase intent ≥ 30% AND prestige ranks ≥ 40% of purchase‑intent group, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing premium branding. If neither condition is met, conclude that. Cost: 15000 euros, 4 weeks.

If the test meets the decision rule (purchase intent ≥30% and compatibility ranks ≥60% of purchase-intent group), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing compatibility. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

case.question: Should TOMRA Systems ASA develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing reverse vending machines for deposit return systems and sensor-based sorting machines for retailers, deposit system operators, recyclers, mining companies and food processors? sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Proposition Test: Homeowners vs High-End RV Owners" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to either a homeowners group (n=300) or a high‑end RV group (n=300). Each group sees a product description of an integrated thermal management kit for RVs/motorhomes, priced 20% above a generic equivalent. Homeowners are asked to state primary purchase reasons (comfort, safety, convenience, brand). High‑end RV owners are asked the same, plus willingness to pay a premium. A decision rule: if homeowners report comfort/safety as primary reason and purchase intent is at least 15% higher than the generic group, T1 is supported. If high‑end RV owners report performance/brand premium and purchase intent is at least 15% higher than the generic group, T2 is supported. If neither group meets its threshold, the theory is not supported.. Sample: 300 homeowners and 300 high‑end RV owners, recruited via an online panel to match demographics.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and primary purchase reason (open‑ended). Secondary measure: willingness to pay a premium (binary: would pay more).. Predictions: T1: Homeowners will report comfort/safety as primary reason and have purchase intent at least 15% higher than the generic group.; T2: High‑end RV owners will report performance/brand premium and have purchase intent at least 15% higher than the generic group.. Decision rule: If homeowners meet the comfort/safety threshold and their intent is at least 15% higher than the generic group, T1 is supported. If high‑end RV owners meet the performance/brand threshold and their intent is at least 15% higher than the generic group, T2 is supported. If neither group meets its threshold, neither theory is supported.. Cost: 2000 euros, 6 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Hobbyist Willingness-to-Pay Survey" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from a panel of hobbyists and small-scale producers. They are shown a mock product description of a compact spinning machine (e.g., a mini card spinning machine) and asked to indicate their maximum price they would pay and the features they would accept. The survey also includes a willingness-to-pay question for a premium version with additional features.. Sample: Proposed sample: 300 participants (150 hobbyists and 150 small-scale producers) recruited via an online panel. Stratified by age, gender, and geographic region to ensure diversity.. Measure: Primary measure: average willingness-to-pay (WTP) for the compact spinning machine. Secondary measure: share of participants who would pay a premium over a baseline price of CHF 200.. Predictions: T1: Average WTP will be above CHF 200, and at least 30% of participants will indicate a premium price.; T2: Average WTP will be below CHF 200, and fewer than 20% of participants will indicate a premium price.. Decision rule: If average WTP is above CHF 200 and at least 30% indicate a premium price, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If average WTP is below CHF 200 and fewer than 20% indicate a premium price, do not invest in a consumer proposition. If the average WTP is between CHF 150 and CHF 200, conduct a follow-up survey to understand the reasons for the lower price sensitivity.. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

case.question: Should Brembo N.V. develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing brake systems for vehicle manufacturers and replacement parts for the aftermarket? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for High‑Performance Brake Kits" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) heritage/adjustability messaging emphasizing 50‑year motorsport heritage, market‑leading adjustability, and Italian design; (B) safety/durability messaging emphasizing proven off‑road performance, extreme‑condition reliability, and racing pedigree. Both groups see the same product description (Brembo GR‑PRO mountain‑bike brake kit) and are asked: "How much would you pay for this kit?" (. Sample: 300 individual mountain‑bikers and off‑road enthusiasts recruited via cycling forums and social media, balanced across age, gender, and riding experience.. Measure: Average willingness‑to‑pay (EUR) for the kit in each group.. Predictions: T1: Group A will report a higher average willingness‑to‑pay than Group B because heritage and adjustability justify premium pricing.; T2: Group B will report a higher average willingness‑to‑pay than Group A because safety and durability in extreme conditions justify premium pricing.. Decision rule: If Group A’s average willingness‑to‑pay exceeds Group B’s by at least €150 (a 10% premium over the €750 price point), we conclude T1 is more likely. If Group B’s average exceeds Group A’s by at least €150, we conclude T2 is more likely. If the difference is less than €150, we conclude both theories are uncertain and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically compare heritage/adjustability messaging against safety/durability messaging. The test will determine whether consumers are willing to pay a premium for heritage-driven kits, which would support T1, or whether safety/durability messaging drives higher willingness to pay, which would support T2. The €15,000 budget and 12‑week timeline are sufficient‑ Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

New claim: Individual mountain-bikers and motorcycle enthusiasts will purchase premium brake kits because they value a product that demonstrates 50 years of motorsport heritage, market-leading adjustability, and Italian design, leading to willingness to pay a premium price.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Sous Vide vs Bulk Storage" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view two product pages for a differentiated consumer vacuum sealer: one emphasizing sous vide capabilities (professional-grade, liquid sealing, preset modes) and one emphasizing bulk food storage (large capacity, reusable bags, cost savings). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7‑point scale (1‑Very unlikely, 7‑Very likely) and state the primary reason for choosing the product.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1‑90) and primary reason for choosing the product (open‑ended).. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s precision tools because they value reliability and durability for professional‑grade metalwork. Who benefits: Individual DIY metalworkers and small business owners who need high‑accuracy cutting tools.. Why behaviour changes: These users replace generic tools when they encounter failure, wear, or insufficient accuracy, and choose established brands that have a reputation for quality.. How value is captured: Gühring can charge premium prices for precision tools, sell through existing B2B channels, and leverage its brand trust to attract non‑industrial buyers.. Assumptions: Hobbyists and small workshops are willing to pay a premium for professional‑grade tools.; Gühring’s current B2B distribution can reach these buyers.; There is measurable demand for precision metalworking tools among this segment.. Predictions: If offered at a 20 % premium over generic alternatives, at least 10 % of surveyed hobbyists will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales of Gühring tools in the consumer‑oriented B2B channel will increase by €50,000 annually within the next 12 months..

T2: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s precision tools because they seek a single source for high‑quality metalworking needs, reducing procurement complexity. Who benefits: Individual DIY metalworkers and small business owners who need a comprehensive set of tools from a single brand.. Why behaviour changes: These users prefer brands that offer a full product portfolio, eliminating the need to source multiple suppliers, and trust a single brand for consistency and support.. How value is captured: Gühring can bundle tools into kits, sell through existing B2B channels, and charge a premium for the convenience of a single‑source solution.. Assumptions: Hobbyists and small workshops value time‑saving and reduced supplier overhead.; Gühring’s current B2B distribution can package and sell kits to individual buyers.; There is measurable demand for a full‑tool‑set solution among this segment.. Predictions: If offered a 15 % discount on a bundled kit of 10 tools, at least 15 % of surveyed hobbyists will indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales of Gühring kits in the consumer‑oriented B2B channel will increase by €30,000 annually within the next 12 months..

Test "Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 200 hobbyists and small workshop owners recruited via metalworking forums and social media, balanced by experience level (beginner, intermediate, advanced).. Measure: 1) Choice: premium-priced Gühring precision tool vs. generic alternative (20% price premium). 2) WTP: maximum price hobbyists would pay for a premium tool. 3) Single-source intent: likelihood to purchase a bundled kit of 10 tools (15% discount).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of respondents will choose the premium Gühring tool and indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks, with a WTP of at least €150 for a single tool.; T2: At least 30% of respondents will choose the bundled kit and indicate intent to purchase within 12 weeks, with a WTP of at least €1,200 for the kit.. Decision rule: If the proportion choosing the premium tool ≥ 30% AND the average WTP ≥ €150, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists. If the proportion choosing the bundled kit ≥ 30% AND the average WTP ≥ €1,200, proceed to develop a single-source kit proposition. If neither condition is met, . Cost: 15000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed hobbyist purchase intent test (X1) to gather evidence on willingness to pay and demand before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Each segment sees a product description of a Rieter spinning machine tailored to their specific use case (e.g., hobbyist: compact, easy-to-operate kit; small-scale: modular, 50 spindles configuration). Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay and likelihood to purchase.. Sample: 500 respondents: 250 hobbyists (aged 25-55, self-identified crafters) and 250 small-scale producers (own fewer than 20 animals, produce less than 50 pounds of fiber). Recruited via craft and small-farm forums.. Measure: Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in Swiss francs and binary purchase intent (yes/no).. Predictions: T1: Hobbyists will show WTP at least 20% higher than small-scale producers and purchase intent at least 15% higher.; T2: Small-scale producers will show WTP at least 15% higher than hobbyists and purchase intent at least 15% higher.. Decision rule: If hobbyist WTP exceeds small-scale producer WTP by at least 20% and both segments show purchase intent above 60%, proceed with a differentiated hobbyist kit. If small-scale producer WTP exceeds hobbyist WTP by at least 20% and both show purchase intent above 60%, proceed with a differentiated small-scale machine. If neither segment meets its threshold, do not expand.. Cost: 8000 euros, 6 weeks.

sources.excerpt: FoodSaver® is the world’s #1 vacuum sealing system that helps avoid waste by keeping food fresher, longer. For over 30 years, FoodSaver has introduced innovative vacuum sealers, bags, and accessories to help people around the world avoid food waste, enjoy their food at its freshest, and save thousands of dollars each year.
Baseline chamber machines are therefore the ideal vacuum packaging solution for butchers´shops, restaurants, hotels, chees dairies, direct marketing companies and farm shops.

The bacterium Clostridium botulinum is able to grow and produce a harmful toxin in the absence of oxygen. It is important that vacuum-packed chilled foods have the necessary controlling factors or hurdles in place to minimise the risk of growth and toxin production by this organism, throughout the shelf-life of the product.

MULTIVAC tabletop chamber machines can be used very flexibly due to their compact dimensions. This means they are an ideal packaging solution for butchers, cheese dairies, restaurants, hotels, direct sellers and supermarkets as well as for a wide range of consumer goods.

sources.excerpt: With a DIY and consumer range of more than 2,000 products, our brands are trusted for a wide range of applications. Our presence extends over 120 countries, allowing us to service retailers worldwide.

Sika is a specialty chemicals company with a globally leading position in the development and production of systems and products for bonding, sealing, damping, reinforcing, and protection in the building sector and industry. Sika has subsidiaries in 103 countries around the world, produces in over 400 factories, and develops innovative technologies for customers worldwide.

Explore Sika’s range of DIY sealants, designed to deliver professional results for home improvement and maintenance projects. Suitable for a variety of interior and exterior applications, these easy-to-use products offer excellent adhesion, flexibility and durability on common building surfaces.

Sika’s specialized solutions (e.g., roofing systems, industrial flooring, structural adhesives) often require trained applicators and strict adherence with technical standards. These products are not marketed for DIY or general retail because improper application could lead to performance failures or safety hazards.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify TOMRA Systems ASA investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings (reverse vending machines for deposit return systems and sensor-based sorting machines for waste, metal recycling, mining, and food processing).. Constraints: Limited to publicly available information; financial and contractual details may not be public.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Need to verify current reach to individual buyers and identify specific consumer use cases.; Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a clear path to consumers, not just product capability.. Alternatives: 1) Develop a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine for residential or small‑business deposit return, sold directly to consumers or via retailers.; 2) Create a subscription‑based recycling service using TOMRA sensors to collect and sort consumer‑generated waste at home or in buildings.; 3) Partner with retailers or housing associations to install TOMRA sensors in public spaces (e.g., shopping malls, office buildings) for consumer‑generated sorting and recycling.; 4) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on existing B2B customers and existing product lines..

T1: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine (or digital refund app) if they receive a clear financial incentive (e.g., instant digital refund) and the convenience of drop‑off or home collection. Who benefits: Individual consumers seeking quick, easy refunds for empty containers.. Why behaviour changes: Current consumer deposit return methods (e.g., bag drop, redemption centers) are often inconvenient and delayed; a direct digital payout removes the need for physical exchange, eliminating the barrier of time and effort.. How value is captured: TOMRA would capture value by charging a small per‑container fee for digital refunds, earning recurring revenue from each consumer transaction.. Assumptions: Consumers are motivated by instant cash value rather than longer‑term recycling goals.; Digital refund platforms can be integrated into existing deposit return ecosystems (retailers, deposit operators) without major infrastructure changes.; Consumers trust the security and reliability of digital refund processes.. Predictions: In a test offering instant digital refunds, consumer participation rate will be higher than a control group receiving traditional refund methods.; Average refund amount per transaction will be similar to existing refund amounts, indicating price sensitivity is modest..

T2: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine (or digital refund app) if they receive a social or environmental reward (e.g., points toward sustainability goals, community credit) in addition to the financial refund, leveraging peer influence and shared values. Who benefits: Individual consumers who value sustainability and community engagement.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers motivated by environmental impact and social proof are willing to participate in deposit return programs that offer tangible, visible benefits beyond cash refunds, creating a sense of contribution and belonging.. How value is captured: TOMRA would capture value by partnering with sustainability platforms or communities to allocate a portion of the per‑container fee toward community projects, fostering long‑term engagement and brand association.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize sustainability over cash refunds when the environmental impact is clear.; Social proof (e.g., public recognition of recycling contributions) drives participation.; Community platforms can be integrated into the refund process without major technical changes.. Predictions: In a test offering sustainability points, consumer participation rate will be higher than a control group receiving only cash refunds.; Consumers will report higher perceived environmental impact when receiving points, indicating that the social component drives behavior..

Test "Digital Refund vs Sustainability Points Test" between T1; T2. Method: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel arms. In Arm A, participants receive instant digital refund (EUR 0.10 per container) via the myTOMRA app. In Arm B, participants receive instant digital refund plus a sustainability point system (equivalent to EUR 0.05 per container) that can be redeemed for local community projects (e.g., tree planting, community clean‑up). Each arm runs for 8 weeks; participants must return at least 10 containers during the period. At the. Sample: 200 residents of a mid‑sized city (e.g., Oslo) recruited via local community boards and social media. Stratify by age and household income to ensure diversity. Randomly assign 100 participants to Arm A and 100 to Arm B.. Measure: 1) Number of containers returned per participant in each arm. 2) Conversion rate: proportion of recruited participants who return at least 10 containers. 3) Average refund value per participant (for Arm A only). 4) Proportion of Arm B participants who redeem sustainability points for community projects.. Predictions: T1: Arm A conversion rate ≥ 25% and Arm B conversion rate ≤ 20% (favoring the instant refund).; T2: Arm B conversion rate ≥ 25% and Arm A conversion rate ≤ 20% (favoring the sustainability points).. Decision rule: If Arm A conversion ≥ 25% AND Arm B conversion ≤ 20%, proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on instant digital refunds (support T1). If Arm B conversion ≥ 25% AND Arm A conversion ≤ 20%, proceed to develop a consumer proposition focused on sustainability points (support T2). If neither threshold is met, recommend no consumer expansion. If both. Cost: 12000 euros, 8 weeks.
